967.title: The great encyclopedia
967.hook: Kahn Singh Nabha compiled the Mahan Kosh, a vast Sikh encyclopedia
967.howItsDone: Sikh readers, students and translators use Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha's Mahan Kosh to look up words, names and places from the Guru Granth Sahib and other Sikh writings, in print and in digital editions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhai Kahn Singh's small book, Ham Hindu Nahin: distinct, and kind. Today, the same man, and a much bigger book.

A word in a hymn stops a reader cold. It's old. It might be Persian, or Sanskrit, or a Punjabi word nobody in the village uses anymore. The granthi doesn't know it. The uncle who knows everything doesn't know it either. Where do you go? For Sikh readers in the time of the reform movement, the answer was slowly being built, one entry at a time, by a scholar from the princely state of Nabha: a book that could say what a word means.
screen: `AN OLD WORD IN A HYMN.` → `NOBODY KNOWS IT.` → `A SCHOLAR STARTS A BOOK.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Kahn Singh's book is called the Mahan Kosh. Mahan means great. Kosh means a store, a treasury, and in Punjabi it's the word for a dictionary. Its full title calls it a sea of jewels of the Guru's word. Second, what's inside. It isn't only a dictionary. It gathers the words of the Guru Granth Sahib and the other Sikh writings, and alongside them people, places, gurdwaras, ragas, weapons, plants and customs. Look up a name from the Gurus' lives and you find who that person was. Look up a raga and you find the musical setting. Look up an ordinary word and you may find how it's used in a hymn. Third, the patience. Tradition says Kahn Singh spent many years on it, checking each entry against the texts. On a page of it today, the care shows: short entries, cross-references, a scholar who wanted readers to find their own way. Fourth, why it matters. Sikhs often point out that the Gurus sang in the speech of their own listeners, not in a scholars' language. Guru Nanak's hymns speak of the word, the shabad, as what carries a person across. But words drift, and a hymn that was plain to its first listeners can turn foggy. A book like the Mahan Kosh clears the fog, so the hymn can speak plainly again. Sikh readers and translators still reach for it. The reformers of the Singh Sabha years wanted Sikhs to know who they were. Kahn Singh's answer was practical: know your own words.

968.title: Macauliffe, the translator
968.hook: an Irish civil servant resigned his post to translate the Granth, working with Sikh scholars
968.howItsDone: Sikh readers and students still consult Macauliffe's English renderings of the Gurus' hymns, alongside modern translations and the original Gurmukhi, and his name comes up when Sikhs talk about early English translations of their scripture.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mahan Kosh, Kahn Singh's great treasury of words. Today, a man who needed Kahn Singh's help to understand those words.

A British official in the Punjab has a safe career: a salary, a rank, a pension waiting at the end. Max Arthur Macauliffe, an Irishman in the Indian Civil Service, had all of that. Then he did something a career like that rarely makes room for. He resigned. He gave up the post, and the security, to spend his days sitting with Sikh scholars over the hymns of the Gurus, trying to carry them into English.
screen: `A SAFE CAREER IN THE PUNJAB.` → `HE RESIGNS.` → `TO SIT WITH THE HYMNS.`

segments.voice: First, what he was up against. The Guru Granth Sahib is sung poetry, in several languages and dialects, set to ragas. An earlier English translation had already come out, and Sikh critics felt it misunderstood the Gurus. A text like that doesn't open easily to an outsider with a dictionary. Second, how he chose to work. Macauliffe didn't translate alone and announce his results. He worked with Sikh scholars, and one name that comes up is Bhai Kahn Singh Nabha. He would put a line into English, and they would talk through what it meant to the people who sang it. Third, the cost. Leaving the service meant giving up income and standing. Accounts of his life say he spent much of his own money on the work and died without seeing it repaid. Whatever the exact sums, the shape of the choice is clear: a comfortable post on one side, a long, uncertain labor on the other, and he chose the labor. Fourth, why it still matters on this path. Translations made in Macauliffe's time are old enough that anyone can now share them freely. When a course like this one wants to quote the Gurus in English, his is one of the versions it is free to use. And there's a quieter lesson. A translator stands between two languages and belongs fully to neither. The good ones know they need help, and ask for it.

969.title: Six volumes, 1909
969.hook: The Sikh Religion was checked by Sikh scholars before it was published
969.howItsDone: Macauliffe's The Sikh Religion is still read by students of Sikh history and scripture, and because it is now in the public domain, its English renderings of the Gurus' hymns are freely quoted and shared.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Macauliffe, the official who gave up his post for the hymns. Today, what all that labor turned into.

Before a word went to the printer, it went to the scholars. That was the method Macauliffe describes. He could have trusted his own ear; he'd lived with the hymns for years by then. Instead, he did something slower and humbler. He showed his English to learned Sikhs, let them argue with it, and changed it when they found a mistake. The result came out in six volumes, under the plain title The Sikh Religion.
screen: `TO THE SCHOLARS FIRST.` → `LET THEM ARGUE WITH IT.` → `THEN, SIX VOLUMES.`

segments.voice: First, what the volumes hold. The full title names three things: the Gurus, the sacred writings, and the authors. So it isn't a bare translation. It tells the lives of the Gurus and the Bhagats, the saints whose hymns sit in the Granth, and sets their verses into that story. A reader meets Guru Nanak's words inside Guru Nanak's life. Second, the checking. Macauliffe himself describes submitting his translations to Sikh scholars and gyanis, the learned readers of the scripture, and asking for their corrections. A translation the community's own experts had read and challenged was a different thing from one an outsider had simply guessed at. Third, why that mattered then. In the reform years, Sikhs were working hard to say clearly who they were. A book in English, read by officials and scholars far beyond the Punjab, could either help or hurt. Checked this way, it put a Sikh reading of the Sikh faith in front of English readers. Fourth, the true thing over the comfortable one. The Gurus ask for the truth to be lived, not just spoken. In Japji, Guru Nanak asks how a person becomes truthful, and answers that it comes through walking in the Lord's will. Checking your work with someone who knows more is a small way of choosing the true thing over the comfortable one. It costs pride. It saves mistakes that could outlast you.

970.title: Bhai Vir Singh
970.hook: a poet and novelist whose writing renewed Punjabi literature
970.howItsDone: Bhai Vir Singh's poems and novels are read in Punjabi schools and Sikh homes, his commentaries are consulted by students of Gurbani, and his house in Amritsar is kept as a memorial.

segments.voice: Yesterday, six volumes, checked by Sikh scholars before print. Today, a writer from Amritsar who worked the other way: not translating out of Punjabi, but writing into it.

Some careful scholarship of the reform years came from people writing in English, for English readers. Bhai Vir Singh made a different bet. He wrote in Punjabi, in Gurmukhi letters, for Punjabis: poems, novels, commentaries, tracts, a newspaper. His work reads like a conviction that a people renews itself through its own language, and that Punjabi could carry beauty and faith as fully as English.
screen: `SCHOLARSHIP IN ENGLISH.` → `HE WROTE IN PUNJABI.` → `RENEWAL IN ITS OWN TONGUE.`

segments.voice: First, the title. Bhai means brother. Sikhs give it to people respected for their learning and devotion, and it stuck to Vir Singh so firmly that it became part of his name. Second, the range. He wrote short lyrics full of nature and longing for the Divine, and a long poem, Rana Surat Singh, about a widowed queen searching for peace. He wrote novels set in the hard years of Sikh history, commentary on the Gurus' hymns, and worked on editions of older Sikh texts. Some readers call him a father of modern Punjabi literature, though the title is a compliment, not a fact anyone can measure. Third, his tone. In his short poems, the world is full of quiet signs: a flower on a mountainside, the sound of water, a bird. The feeling is longing, and then a glimpse of nearness. It echoes the Gurus' own hymns, where Guru Nanak speaks of the creation as the place the Creator can be seen, dwelling in all of it. Fourth, why renewal. Reformers can argue and organize. But people also need something to love, words to read at night, a story that makes them proud. Vir Singh gave the reform movement poems and novels, and gave Punjabi readers a reason to pick up their own language with joy. He did it with the plainest tool there is: one more line, written in the language his readers dreamed in.

971.title: A novel called Sundri
971.hook: Vir Singh's heroine Sundri gave young Sikhs a story of courage
971.howItsDone: Sundri is still read by Punjabi readers and in Sikh schools, and her story is retold to young Sikhs as an example of courage, service and equality in the Khalsa.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhai Vir Singh, the poet of renewal, writing in Punjabi for Punjabis. Today, one of his novels, and the young woman at its center.

A girl is carried off from her family by a powerful man. Her brother rides after her with a small band of Sikh fighters and brings her back. The obvious ending is a wedding, a quiet house, a safe life. Instead, she chooses the forest. She takes amrit, joins the Khalsa, and lives with the band in the hard years when Sikhs were hunted. She cooks, nurses the wounded, rides, and refuses to be afraid. Her name is Sundri, and she is the heroine of a novel by Bhai Vir Singh.
screen: `CARRIED OFF, BROUGHT BACK.` → `SHE CHOOSES THE FOREST.` → `A NOVEL CALLED SUNDRI.`

segments.voice: First, the setting. Vir Singh set the story in the years of the jathas, the small bands of Sikhs living in forests and hills while they were hunted. Sikh memory calls those years a time of martyrs. Sundri brought that history close, through one young woman's eyes. Second, the heroine. Sundri isn't a decoration in someone else's story. She makes the choices. She takes amrit, receives a new name, and becomes a full member of the Khalsa. She serves in the langar and nurses the wounded. In the novel she even tends to a wounded enemy soldier, because seva, selfless service, doesn't ask which side someone fought on. Third, why a novel. A history book can tell you what happened. A novel lets you live inside someone. This one invites young Sikh readers, girls and boys alike, to walk beside their ancestors in danger, with a woman at the center of the story. For readers in the reform years, this was part of the renewal: not a lecture on faith, but a heroine to admire. Fourth, the Gurus behind it. In Asa di Var, Guru Nanak asks why we should call woman lesser, when from her kings are born. Readers can hear that line in Sundri's story. She lives as an equal in the Khalsa, carries its danger, and keeps its compassion.

972.title: A school for girls
972.hook: at Ferozepur, Bibi Harnam Kaur and Bhai Takht Singh built a school for Sikh girls
972.howItsDone: Sikh communities run and support schools and colleges, many open to girls and boys alike, and the reform-era girls' school at Ferozepur is remembered as part of that story.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sundri, a heroine in a novel. Today, real girls, and a real school.

Ferozepur, a town in the Punjab. A husband and wife have an idea that some of their neighbors think is a waste: a proper school for Sikh girls. Reading, writing, Gurbani, Punjabi, practical skills. Not a few lessons at home, but a school, with teachers and a place to live. They don't have much money. They have a conviction, and a lot of stubbornness. Their names are Bhai Takht Singh and Bibi Harnam Kaur.
screen: `AN IDEA SOME CALLED A WASTE.` → `LITTLE MONEY, MUCH CONVICTION.` → `TAKHT SINGH AND HARNAM KAUR.`

segments.voice: First, the two of them. Takht Singh was a teacher and a man of the Singh Sabha reform. Harnam Kaur was his wife and partner in the work. The school came to be called the Sikh Kanya Mahavidyala: kanya means girl, and a mahavidyala is a great school. Tradition remembers it starting small and growing, one family's trust at a time. Second, how they kept it going. The school ran on gifts, and the story told about Takht Singh is that he traveled and asked for support again and again, collecting for the girls. Harnam Kaur cared for the students who lived there, teaching, cooking, mothering. A school is a building, but it's also a person who stays up when a child is sick. Third, the reason. The reformers wanted Sikhs to know their own scripture and history, and that couldn't stop at the boys. If mothers couldn't read Gurbani, how would the next generation learn it at home? Teaching girls was part of renewing the whole community. Fourth, the Gurus' words underneath. In the Japji, Guru Nanak returns again and again to one word: suniai, by listening. By listening, he sings, sorrow and sin are washed away. The hymn names no one who is barred from listening, and the Gurus' hymns speak to all who listen, women and men alike. A school for girls simply took those hymns at their word.

973.title: The Chief Khalsa Diwan, 1902
973.hook: a central body to coordinate the reform societies
973.howItsDone: The Chief Khalsa Diwan still exists in Amritsar and runs schools and other institutions; Sikh communities today coordinate their work through gurdwara committees, councils and networks of local sangats.

segments.voice: Yesterday, suniai, by listening, and a school for girls at Ferozepur. Today, the end of a week of builders, and the body that tried to tie their work together.

By now the Punjab is full of Singh Sabhas, reform societies in town after town. One runs a school. One prints tracts. One argues with another about how things should be done. Each is doing good work, and each is doing it alone. Sooner or later someone asks the obvious question: what if we did this together? The answer was a central council, based in Amritsar, to coordinate the reform: the Chief Khalsa Diwan.
screen: `SINGH SABHAS EVERYWHERE.` → `EACH WORKING ALONE.` → `WHAT IF, TOGETHER?`

segments.voice: First, the name. Diwan is a word for a council or an assembly; Sikhs also use it for a gathering in the gurdwara where hymns are sung. Khalsa is the community of initiated Sikhs. Chief means it sat above the local societies, a hub for many wheels. Second, what it did. It brought the Singh Sabhas into one network, so a school in one town and a press in another could share plans, teachers and money. It started and supported schools, spoke for Sikhs to the government, and worked on causes like the one you'll hear tomorrow. Among its leaders, one name that comes up is Sundar Singh Majithia. Third, the honest part. Working together isn't the same as agreeing. Some Sikhs felt the Diwan was too cautious with the British, too close to the powerful. Others valued it for getting things done. Both views are part of the story, and later movements grew partly out of that disagreement. Fourth, the week behind it. Kahn Singh, building a treasury of words. Macauliffe, with Sikh scholars checking his six volumes. Bhai Vir Singh and his heroine, Sundri. Takht Singh and Harnam Kaur, and their school for girls. Every one of them needed others. The Gurus called the gathering of the faithful the sangat, and in Gurbani the company of the holy is where a person is lifted. The Diwan was an attempt to turn many good efforts into one sangat.
